title: Rupee Rally Hits Roadblock as Oil and Outflows Test RBI Defence
excerpt: The rupee slipped to 94.98 on Monday as Brent at $114.48, importer hedging and a $75-80 billion RBI defence left the currency pinned near its 95-per-dollar line.
body:
• The rupee fell 5 paise to 94.98 against the dollar in early trade on Monday, October 26, after closing 12 paise lower at 94.93 on Friday — a second straight decline as Brent crude rose 1.92% to $114.48 a barrel.
  • The Reserve Bank of India has deployed an estimated $75 billion to $80 billion in spot dollar sales and swaps since June 8, and forex reserves have fallen to $721.016 billion in the week ended October 16, down $5.011 billion in that week alone.
  • Traders see 95 per dollar as the RBI's soft defence line: the currency briefly strengthened past it after the central bank's October measures, then struggled to sustain gains as importer hedging and portfolio outflows rebuilt dollar demand.
  • For readers sending money to India or holding rupee costs, the near-term range matters more than the headline: at 94.98, $1,000 converts to about Rs 94,980 before fees, and analysts say a sustained move will need lower oil, not just intervention.

The rupee's recovery is losing steam. The currency traded in a narrow range on Monday and fell 5 paise to 94.98 against the U.S. dollar in early trade, weighed down by elevated crude oil prices and geopolitical tensions in West Asia, according to PTI reporting in The Hindu BusinessLine.

At the interbank foreign exchange market, the rupee opened at 94.92 and then slipped to 94.98, extending Friday's 12-paise fall to 94.93. The dollar index was softer, trading at 101.49, down 0.15%, and U.S. Treasury yields eased — factors that cushioned the downside but did not reverse it. The Sensex dropped 536.30 points to 72,583.86 in early trade and the Nifty fell 200.10 points to 22,402.80.

Why the rally stalled

The stall follows a sharp, policy-driven rebound. On October 12, the rupee rose about 1% in a single session — its best day since April — after the RBI announced measures to temper dollar demand, redirecting oil companies' dollar purchases away from the spot market and tightening hedging rules, Reuters reported via Kitco News. The oil window alone was expected to take about $10 billion to $12 billion of monthly dollar demand out of the spot market.

That relief met an immediate test. Sharp gains drew hedging-related flows into the non-deliverable forward market, linked to foreign portfolio investments, a senior trader at a foreign bank told Reuters. Importers who had pushed forward dollar purchases to record levels in September stepped up hedging again when premiums fell, rebuilding the very demand the measures were meant to curb.

"Unless BoP pressures ease more broadly, gradual INR depreciation is likely to resume once their initial impact fades."

— ANZ analysts, via Reuters

The cost of the defence

The defence has been expensive. Economists and traders at six banks estimate the RBI has deployed around $75 billion to $80 billion through spot sales and dollar-rupee sell/buy swaps since June 8 — about half the more than $140 billion it mobilised through special measures earlier this year, according to Reuters reporting summarised by Outlook Business.

The drawdown is visible in the weekly reserves data. Reserves fell to $721.016 billion in the week ended October 16, after a $8.578 billion drop to $726.027 billion in the previous week. That compares with $734.6 billion through October 2, about $51 billion below the peak in the first week of September.

Forex traders on Monday echoed that tension. Anuj Choudhary, Research Analyst at Mirae Asset Sharekhan, said the rupee opened slightly lower on elevated crude and Middle East tensions, with softness in the dollar cushioning the fall, and expected a slight negative bias as foreign investor selling and oil prices pressured the currency, offset only if the RBI intervened again.

Oil is the variable the RBI cannot control

India imports most of its crude, so oil is the channel through which a Middle East shock becomes a rupee shock. Brent at $114.48 on Monday keeps the import bill high and importers' dollar demand firm, even when the broader dollar is weak. Reuters noted a week earlier, in coverage carried by BusinessLine, that the rupee has oscillated around 95, briefly strengthening past it before struggling to sustain the move — a pattern traders read as the RBI selling dollars to limit weakness past that level.

Foreign investors were net buyers of Rs 887.65 crore of equities on Friday, exchange data showed, but portfolio outflows of more than $30 billion from local stocks so far in 2026 remain a persistent pain point cited by traders.

What to watch

Three signals will decide whether 95 holds: Friday's reserves release, Brent — a retreat from the $110s would ease importer demand faster than any curb — and hedging costs. Until at least two turn, the rupee is likely to stay pinned near 95.
